projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Elmer R. Cheh was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of Elmer R. Cheh. Mr. Cheh serviced with the U.S army's 24th Division field artillery battery C. He service in the Pacific theatre and his highest rank was corporal. I am Thomas Swope and we recorded this at the home of Mr. Cheh's home in Hyrum Ohio on October 25, 2001. Mr. Cheh's age at the time of the recording was 78.

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Lets see I got drafted into the service January 1943 and I got out of service April 1946 so that's- - what else do we want to know?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What branch of the service was this?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Well lets see I went to Columbus, over there, then they sent me to Camp Carson, Colorado in a mule pack they wanted people that were 6 feet tall that handle - - we were field artillery unit we'd brake the guns down into six pieces and climb mountains with it, so we were climbing the Rocky Mountains of Denver over there and then we did our training there and then they decided they wanted to make ski troops so they issued us snow tents, skis and all the winter stuff and we were going to go to Camp Hail, Colorado and train over there and then they change their mind at the last minute I guess, because of the European theatre was more or less drawing to a close so then we - - they made us motorized field artillery they took away our 75 howitzers and gave us 105's and we - - that was in the 71st division at Camp Carson. And we trained with 105 howitzers I was a corporal, a gunner corporal in charge of firing battery and then we after that they wanted replacements and I was sent over seas to another out fit in New Guinea where I joined the 24th infantry corp. as an instrument corporal and from there - - from New Guinea we went to the invasion of Lete and then we got through at late and we went to Mendoro, and the to - - Mendenow and that's - -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go to New Guinea about when was that?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Lets see I trained in the United States for it was almost 8 to 12 months I was at Camp Carson over there and then I went to I got shipped to New Guinea, Port Moresby we got off the ship and they I remember getting on one of these floating amphipean alligators and then they took me off the ship on that and while we were going to shore over there, something happened with the rudder and we were zigzagging all over the place until the guy got down in the back with us and started guiding us toward the shore he was working that rudder by hand from underneath he was peeking up over the top looking where we were going finally we made it to shore and in New Guinea we got indoctrination over there we - - new Guinea was secure by then mostly and the we started getting prepared for the laatee invasion and lets see on the laatee invasion I was I went on the LCI with the forward observers and I was with the forward observers party mostly we - - I was coordinating the field artillery with the targets and let's see in Laatee that was - what happened over there that was all I could remember was going through the jungles over there it was wet and hot and mosquitoes and everything else and lets see that's when I was - - I can't remember exactly were I was on a LST that one time coming in on invasion and I think that was Men Doro and a shell came through the side of a ship where I was in the back of the ship over looking the deck were the vehicles were stored and it hit gasoline drums right at my feet and fortunately it was a dud it just blew open the tank the gasoline drums a spray of gasoline hit the foot but it didn't explode I was fortunate over there so I went back to the crews quarters and got into the shower and washed myself off because I started feeling a little tingling and the one area it starting to burn my skin and then the ship started listing a little bit so we had to pull back out and then we came in the next day after they repaired the holes in the ship I guess we was taken out of water and then we just went through medoora going through the jungles and then lets see one time we were going up a trail and then it was actually a road and we came upon a truck and it was parked it was headed into the woods and we could see the mans head in through the rear window and we had Filipino scoots with us and he knew Japanese so he was just trying to get this Japanese person to come out of the truck and I guess he wouldn't so a couple of guys took aim and fired and blew the back of his head off. And that was pretty scary and then we kept going there and we came to town a large clearing and we could see through over a between a valley there was another plateau and we were on one platue and there's a valley and there was another platue and we see a bad japans encampment there on the other side over there and apparently we took them by surprise and we just started settling in and we were going to start firing over there and all the Japanese saw us and they took off running over there and we got down there and came to their barracks and so they had a bat in there and everything so I don't know where they went but we didn't see em any more and lets see what else. There's another time on patrol that I had a close call we were camped on a knoll for some reason the top of this knoll all the trees was cut down it was a bare knoll and there's a little shack on the top of it that was one of the Filipinos places of residence or something it was just a small shack and all at once machine guns started opening up on us over there and I could see everybody hit the ground dirt and we were laying there and I saw the machine gun pattern come across the ground and across the guys rear-end and they got him over there I had jumped down and tried to crawl in underneath this little shack cause it raised off the ground so only about a foot high I just couldn't make it under there was trying to crawl under there I was trying to crawl inside my helmet, but that was another time. Lets see one other time I was I had just gotten cleaned up my uniform I was nice and clean and dry and I was walking through the compound and all at once a sniper started shooting at me I could feel bullets were hitting around me and there was a foxhole alright right next to me but it was full of water so I wasn't about to jump in there and get all wet again but about the third shot out there I jumped in the water and so got away from him and I guess that same sniper he came into camp that night while we were all sleeping and some how he got on top of one those 6 by 6's and there was a 30 caliber machine-gun mounted on the thing and it was the kitchen GMC and then he started opening up with that I think he shot up that whole kitchen I don't think there's a pot and pan left whole over there by the next morning there he took off and I guess nobody wanted to fire at him, because the didn't want to expose their position that's the only reason why I can't understand why nobody shot at him so the next morning we went on patrol and looking for him and we found him he was sleeping oh I don't know how far away we walked quite a ways into the jungle and we found him sleeping at the base of the tree over there covered with a poncho and his head and everything was covered and their army ponchos he had with him and GI stuff and I'll tell you everybody just laid back and filled him full of holes and I never saw anything like it he just - - there was nothing left of him but he had GI canteen and GI poncho and other American equipment on him I don't know he must have got it off some dead soldier or something. Mr. Swope: A 6x6 truck?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Yeah, that's their kitchen they were carrying all the kitchen equipment. Let's see there was - - I was in one of those Japanese bonsai attacks we had a, we had a hill this is in Medora also and the Japanese attacked and they somehow they took one-half the hill and we had the other half it was no more than a hundred and fifty yards difference between the whole top of the hill and I could hear one of the GI's are calling for mortar fire all the time to repel the Japanese attacking on that side fortunately I was on the other side of the hill from where they were attacking and then, but the Japanese took that side of the hill and I could hear one Japanese soldier yelling "sugeets"? sugets or something I don't know but I think he was calling somebody and I don't know what happened but in the morning we got called up a small tank with a 75 Howitzer on it and he blasted that side of the hill and we got the hill back over there and I was going down through the trenches there looking at em and some of em Japanese where still alive These infantry over there no remorse or no pity they just shot em one of these soldiers over there he finally saw this Japanese I saw him and he had a big round face and he looked up at the GI and I saw him kind of smile, but this GI got the butt of his M1 and just smashed his face in, but it's kind of scary, so, but I was wondering what that hill looks like nowadays just to see and go back and look at what it is I know when we came through these towns in the Philippines over there we were going through they were ordinary just looking on long, long stilts, all the homes were they were all on stilts above ground and we were going through it and then when I - - going back through the towns later 2 or 3 weeks or about a month later it was so completely different the jaz had strung wire all over the place they were just hanging from all the palm trees it just looked completely different I just couldn't get over it and let's see then we were getting ready to after we took these 3 laatee, mendenow and mendora we were going to make the big push on Japan, so I - - I was pretty good at drawing and everything so they had me lay out a scamatic for all the LST's and how we are going to load them onto the ships and so I drew up a scale model of things and then we laid it out on the ground and how we were going to park all the vehicles on the LST's and get going over there and we had it all set up to go we loaded all the ships up and we spent the night in our pup-tent mosquito net on this beach over there and shove off in the morning and then they dropped the Adam-Bomb and they called it of and so then we went drew back into the camp and got some R & R and that's when I got hurt I broke my ankle I was running through the compound and stepped on a coconut and broke my ankle and they said no sense taking care of you here and they sent me home I got home 6 months earlier then the rest of my outfit just because I had broken a ankle.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were just running you weren't running from anything?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: No, no I wasn't I was probably running for chow or something and then I got home six months early that was that was about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your unit?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: It was 24th Infantry 21st combat team Battery B field artillery 105 Howitzers and in fact three of us just got together after fifty years lets see yeah it was fifty years, there's James Harless he lives in Illinois, lets see where is Harry Truman's?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Independence

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Independence, Missouri that's where he lives. There's another Cooper he's from Texas and he moved to Illinois and he was real close to James Harless and then Powell Barlow in Anaheim, California and he got invited so the four of us got together at Jims house over there he contacted all of the and so I drove there and Powell Barlow flew in he was on his way to visit relatives in Kentucky and Cooper was just an hour or two away from where they lived so we had a reunion the 4 of us. And that was nice the only one I would have recognized was Powell Barlow all the others changed a lot especially Cooper he was just a small guy he was you know somebody you wouldn't pay that much attention to, but he was big and he filled out he looked real happy and he and his wife came and Powell Barlow he was really the only one I would have recognized when he got off the plane we went to meet him at the airport and I recognized him right away and Jimmy Harless he hadn't changed to much but I would have recognized him if I would have studied him more I asked them if I looked any different and they said yeah you filled out too. We just - - in fact I just talked to Jim Harless on the phone a couple weeks ago my wife picked up a book at the library about the Philippines the camps they were prisoner of war camps and she was over there and she was enthralled with it and I read it too and after I read it we sent it to him and told him to send it on to Cooper and Barlow and let them read it and Harless is still reading it and he called back and told us how he was enjoying the book and so that's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So as an observer how close to the enemy line did you get?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Right up front in fact there was - - I was up there a couple times I could see what the infantry goes through over there and then when I came back somebody else took my place and then whoever took my place he was laying right next to the lieutenant who was in charge and he had a sniper fire hit right in the forehead, so that could have been me and so I was pretty fortunate I came out with a busted ankle that's all, well I did catch malaria that's it so I landed in Crowell hospital got malaria over there and that's about all I had wrong with me but it was an experience it was a - -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How would you communicate back obviously looking for concentrations of the enemy troops how would you communicate back?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Radio. Regular radio. Yeah sound phones they used sound phones, but radio to get back up in lines we were about what I'd say about three miles in front of our battery at least. Oh there was one time we were on mendinow that was a relatively easy, easy one to go to we would have no opposition going in and we went in there and we joined up with some Philippine gorilla's and I was assigned to one, one forward observer party and we went to a back up into the hill's with these Philippine gorillas scouting out these concentrations of Japanese we never did see any, but that was nice duty up there because we didn't have no problems and I learned how to play Mah-Jongg, the officers where playing Mah-Jongg all the time and I kind of watching me playing so ah green dragon and yellow dragon and stuff like that I had forgotten how it went anymore it's been so long, but I remember one time I took the jeep with one other fellow and we went to get some water and we were coming down a trail and we could see about a half mile ahead over there and we saw two figures on the trail over there and I wasn't sure who they were and I told the this buddy next to me to watch over there I saw somebody so I'm gonna give it the race past so we raced passed and nothing happened and later on we found it was phillipino gorillas just scouting around so that was nice duty over there that was the best part of the whole thing I think.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about the Filipinos people what where they like?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: They were nice there was one married couple that we - - I got acquainted with they invited us to their home it was just a small little shack in the jungle there clearing and they had a piano and she could play and we were playing and she was playing a song let's see what song were we singing "Always" yeah that's the song we were singing "Da Da Daa and always - -" I remember that song particularly it almost brought tears to my eyes but that was nice it they would tell us about the Japanese occupation over there and they had to put up with em and it wasn't any fun, but we got through it and most of survived and I lost a couple of my buddies over there I remember let's see Aquino Yeah he was on a patrol once over there and he was riding in a jeep with a couple other guys and submachine gun opened up on em and they got everybody in the jeep and U.P. Adams he was from Montgomery, Alabama he got shot he was on patrol that one time and he was a nice guy. What else is there, there's so many things that happened over there it's been what forty, fifty some years it's been more then that fifty six, fifty seven years ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The invasion of Lete Gulf

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: What was that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: the invasion of Lete Gulf was that early forty-five?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Yeah, let's see I got a picture here LST right on the beach there here's side by side I remember that the LST couldn't get to close up to the beach up there and making sand bags to make a ramp and I was one of the soldiers out there with a ramp with sand bags and I remember the ramp was down on the LST and it was right over my head I was waiting for a big wave and pushed the LST and I'd be buried out there with them sand bags, but it turned out o.k. and we got ashore and I think that was at latee.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Doing anything with your buddies for entertainment to relieve tension or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Well we used to there was a we saw movies every onced in a while, I remember that one time we had gone at night up there's the bomber squadron at the airport a landing strip over there and they were showing movies that night so we took on em must have been a half mile or a mile a way over there and we walked a mile just to see a movie and then I remember they had the USO that one time Bob Hope was suppose to be there but I was so far back that I couldn't even have recognized em there was so many of us and I was so far in the back that we could hear the music and the talking but I could hardly make out the figures on the stage it was just to far away an so other then entertainment there wasn't to much entertainment.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What about letters from home?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Letters that we always looked forward to that oh that one time when I was over with the Philippine gorillas I got a package from my mother and they were dropping us supplies from a Piper-cub and the guy was working the radio at the time and the pilot says I got a package here for Elmer Cheh here and he says okay I'll get it he swooped down low and dropped it over there and it almost landed on top of me, but it landed a few feet away from me and I ran over and picked it up and here it was leaking and I could smell booze I hurried and got my canteen cup out of there and got about a half a cup out of it and see sent me a bottle of Seagram's V.O. and we all took a sip of it and I told the pilot over there and he said if he would have know that he wouldn't have dropped it he would have kept it himself, that was funny. She had it wrapped in popcorn and everything but that drop from the plane over there was a little bit too much for it. Let's see what else was there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of the day the Japanese attacked Pear Harbor?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: I was - - when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor I was still in school, but I was selling papers at the time up on Shakers Square but em a special edition came out so they gave us a bunch of em walking up and down streets in Shaker Heights selling papers over there and that war was declared over there I remember selling that doing that but I think, but after I graduated school the army said come on we need you and so I think I had about a week over there after I graduated and I was inducted, so that was in forty-three and I think it was forty-one when they dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your hometown back then?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: In Cleveland, up on Buckeye Road in Cleveland. So then I went to East Tech high School there I was training for aeronautics, so that was my specialization course so I told them when I got inducted over there I'd like to go into aeronautics or somewhere so they put me in a mule pack they wanted people 6 feet and over to work with howitzers and load the howitzers on the mule packs and stuff so that was the - - so I didn't get in I tried to apply to get in the air corp. in Colorado, but before the transfer came through I got shipped out so I never did get out, but after I got out of the service I got my flying gun I took a G.I. Bill and got my pilots license over at ?Chagrin Falls and took my training and that was fun. I was just getting on the plane over there I think I soloed after a 8 hours instruction I remember that first time over there with the instructor we were making shoot take offs and landings and he said stop the stop over here and he got out of the plane and he said okay take off, so that was my first solo and that was exciting so I took off and flew around a little bit and came back down and they took the cross country training, instrument training and so then I got an extension on that, and so I got my flying in after all and that was fun. I remember my brother-in-law Joe he wanted to take flying took training and he was a scared of heights so I don't see how he - - but he came down and we were flying together all the time. I remember that one time he landed at Horn's Field and I was waiting up on top I was just circling the field and I see his plane got touched down over there and all at once it tips up nose down I guess he landed the wrong way over there and landed upside down over there and it tipped him over there and he was just pointed on the ground nobody got hurt but the propeller got bent a little bit, but we did a lot of flying I went cross-country I flew to Indiana to visit some friends of ours over there and knocked on their door and surprised them and said hello and spend some time with them and then they drove us back to the airport and we went and took off and went back home again. And then I flew around and went to Pennsylvania and around Sandusky and all around and over Lake Erie and I remember going over and flying over Lake Erie there was these speed boats out there racing and there was on racing along and I remember I got down real low and I chased them around down there and he was zigzagging around the lake and I was ziging and zagging after him and finally got tired of playing over there and wiggled my wings and took off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were probably over in the Philippines the day FDR died do you remember hearing that news?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Yeah, I remember it coming over the announcement on the P.A. system, but I don't even remember where I was at the time, I think I was at mendenow in the last island yeah that surprised everybody quite a bit it was real somber and everybody was just sitting around over there. And just thinking what's going to happen now cause FDR was a good leader, but Truman did a great job. He came in there and knowing business over there I guess I got thank him personally for dropping the bomb cause or else I would have been over there in Japan doing what I don't know so yeah that worked out pretty good for us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction when you heard the bomb had been dropped did you understand what that was about?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Not ah, the only thing was that the invasion was off and I was real happy about that cause I knew the Japanese where if you were going to their home land well they were going to be fighting tooth and nail, but I didn't realize the destruction there that bomb caused on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, that was, that was something else, so I hope we don't have to do that anymore that was a, that was something else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But obviously we were looking at a half million casualties on our side.

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Oh, At least, at least cause we were all set to go and our ships were loaded and I was in my mosquito bar and on the beach over there waiting for daylight just waiting for us to get up and start the invasion and that's when they dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You guys knew that was the next step you were going to Japan, right?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Yeah definitely we were going to Japan they told us we were going to Japan. I don't remember if I was going to be a forward observer on that, party or not probable I was in a forward observer party it was section and it was - -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It must have been a lot of tension for you guys thinking about that?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Yes. Oh yeah you know how you get kind of nervous and worried about it you don't know what's going to happen, before each invasion you start thinking am I going to make it through this one yeah they don't know from what I've seen what happens out there and I've seen dead GI's and I've seen dead Japanese too and it's nothing to take lightly and it makes depression on you. For a long time I didn't talk about it even back in the service I didn't talk about it my wife says even now, now I'm just now starting to talk about it, but I didn't want to talk about it but to anybody, other GI's maybe mention a word or two but it's something, something real personal. And it stays with you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember having specific trouble adjusting right after you got back?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: No not really. I just put it out of my mind. And went about my business I know when we came back with what they called a 52-20 club you got to club for twenty dollars a week and before that and I was getting tired of laying around and I applied for a job and went over to the post office I was going to go over to the gas company cause I had a job doing I was going for a surveying job cause that's what I did before the service and then somebody told me why not try for the post-office too and the post office called me first so I took the test and passed so I started a motor vehicle branch over there and so I took the civil service exam for a carrier and passed that and so I was working as a carrier outside downtown Cleveland for awhile and so I transferred out to ? Falls and then I built this home out here and so that's where I retired from Sagrin falls over there Post office, putting in 33 years in the post office and then so now just Enjoying being out here. I built this house with a lot of help here from the hole in ground all the way to the top so and that was one of my major accomplishments.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think of that whole overseas experience does one thing come to mind as your most vivid memory?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Most vivid memory well when that side of the shell came through the side of the ship and drenched me with gasoline that that was something over there and but em oh what I remember when we were going on invasion and on the fantail of the ship over there we were going looking back over the water and phosphorus in the water and it looked kind of peaceful and the stars in the sky you can count every star it was so clear and bright at night time and was just sitting there in the back of the ship and thinking what's going to happen what's in the future for me what's going to happen if we get though over there and there's a lot of times when I was just before I went overseas at Camp Carson in Colorado at night I would sit out there and just look up at the sky and see the mountains outline the sky you see Will Rogers monument in the mountain there and just sit there and think and what's gonna happen how am I gonna make out and kinda hoping for the best and fortunately it came through okay came made out real well. And then I got married not my? Sweetheart my in fact my wife was introduced to me by my former girlfriend she moved out of town and I was in the hospital at the time with my broken foot my broken ankle and she said why don't you go visit him over there in Crial? and that's how we meet that was love at first sight really that was nice and so she came visit me and when I got out of the hospital we were going together for a long for a while for about a year I guess her parents kept saying it's not good to be going together to long, she was always saying don't wait to long and so I told Jenny I says well I'll get a job if we can find a place to live over there and then we'll get married so before you know it her parents had a double house down there in 138th off of Union and then I accused them of throwing the people out upstairs over there so we could get married so they moved out and we got the place upstairs and we got married.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you did have a girlfriend back home when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Sort of let's see I was going with this girl Betty over there and then Betty and Jenny were real good buddies and did everything they were going to John Hay together and they were chumming along through over there and then when Betty moved a way she told Jenny to- - so she and so she started writing to me and so we were writing and came back here and I meet Jenny and I liked what I saw and apparently she did too so and that's how we and we got together so we a have three kids two boys and a girl the girl first Carol she lives in Niles? and Dennis he is in Savannah, Georgia he's doing real well with gulf stream aerospace and my son Glen he's out in California, Whittier he has his own trucking company business and so all three of our kids are doing real well I'm proud of em. And we got what how many grandchildren and we got one and two and four grandchildren and one great-grand child. So were doing real well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: it sounds like it.

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: Were doing good, I'm satisfied I'm real happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Elmer R. Cheh
sp.p: there's probably more a lot of other things but I can't think of it now. Came home on a furlough a couple of times but they were so short, I don't remember hardly doing anything there was nobody here to talk to most of my buddies were gone and just to be home and see my mom and dad and didn't do anything and stayed here for a while and got relaxed and rested up and went back in and I remember that time when I got discharged when I was in hospital down in chocathe? Ohio, my first stop my malaria acted up because I was off of adabrin? out of quinine in fact I was on furlough then and I got the attack at home and so they rushed me into Criol Hospital my doctor didn't now what malady I had I was cold and hot and cold and hot so I went to criol? Over there and got taken care of over there and then instead of shipping me back to that other hospital - - what did I just say Choicathe? I got discharge form Criol? Hospital. And that's about the end of it there.
